messages.subject: aroma.affymetrix v0.7.2 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi, aroma.affymetrix v0.7.2 is available.  Except from some bug fixes,
the main update is that paired copy-number analysis should work again.

Version: 0.7.2 [2007-09-30]
o Now the main HTML file for ChromosomeExplorer is ChromosomeExplorer.html,
  which is in analogue to how the ArrayExplorer works.  This HTML now
  loads to a different Javascript file with a different name so that
  already existing index.html ChromosomeExplorer files will still work.
o By default, all CopyNumberSegmentationModel plots do now display
  non-robust and robust estimates of the standard deviation of the
  raw CNs across the complete genome.  Note that this is not done
  segment by segment, so if there are alot of aberrations then these
  estimates will be biased.
o BUG FIX: Forgot to update ExonRmaPlm to handle compatibility issues
  with affyPLM/preprocessCore. See below.
o BUG FIX: The CopyNumberSegmentationModel:s did not support paired
  copy-number analysis by specifying references files explictly.
  To do this, pass an additional list of CnChipEffectSet:s via
  constructor argument 'refTuple'.  This list my contain the same
  chip types, and each chip type must contain exactly the same number
  of files.  Note, the hashcode-generated hexadecimal tag added to
  the save CopyNumberSegmentationModel results, but also as part of
  the ChromosomeExplorer image files, will be different in this new
  version, meaning the package will not detect already existing
  segmentation estimates.  You can always one run chromosome, check
  the new hashcode, and rename existing files to have the same one.
o BUG FIX: Before duplicated tags were removed using unique(), but that
  would also remove duplicated tags that were not "neighbors", e.g.
  the 2nd "-X" tags in "ACC,-X,RMA,A+B,FLN,-X" was removed.  Now
  only duplicated neighboring tags are removed, e.g. "-X,-X,-X".
o ROBUSTNESS: Now getAverageFile() of AffymetrixCelSet detects if an
  average file has been deleted between calls and recalculates it,
  if missing.
o BETA: Did some "behind the scenes" restructuring of the
  CopyNumberSegmentationModel by adding an even simpler superclass
  ChromosomalModel, allowing for simpler types of modelling along
  the chromosomes.
o CLEAN UP: Moved several classes to aroma.affymetrix.extras that
  are haven't been updated in a long time and are likely to be broken.
  This was done in order make this package easier to maintain. If this
  broke something for you, please contact me.
o Package pass R CMD check on R v2.6.0 beta and all of the redundancy
  tests.  The redundancy tests are now available under testScripts/
  in the package directory.

As always, see group page for details on how to update/install.

Cheers

Henrik

That could be because I know harmonized code for GLAD and CBS, and
forgot about the GLAD specific column(s).

However, unless you fine tune the GLAD parameters I would not rely
fully on the GLAD 'call':s.  It also depends on what kind of data you
have.  See their paper for more details.

> Moreover, in an older version of this file obtained by fitting the
> gladModel using the robust average of the samples as a reference set,
> I get the following list of breakpoints for chormosome 1, 21 and 22
> from one particular sample:
>
> sample  chromosome      start   stop    mean    count   call
> Bf14203 1       792429  77218238        -0.01   13032   neutral
> Bf14203 1       77219051        77244574        -0.551  5       neutral
> Bf14203 1       77256764        211216828       -0.003  20466 neutral
> Bf14203 1       211218311       211225731       -0.668  2       neutral
> Bf14203 1       211227570       245378187       -0.007  6715 neutral
> Bf14203 21      9887804 46902240        -0.002  7125    neutral
> Bf14203 22      14433758        17005919        0.087   341     gain
> Bf14203 22      17006930        19784562        -0.056  339     neutral
> Bf14203 22      19785571        49519949        0.133   5527 gain
>
> Actually, I am not sure that it is a list of breakpoints since the
> sequence of calls on the first chromosome contain the same state:
> neutral. How can I interpret this list of calls?

See paper.  I believe this is because they call the regions using
pruning an hierarchical clustering trying to find global cut offs from
the data in order to get three states, loss, neutral, and gain.
Again, this is a bit ad hoc and success depends very much on what kind
of data you have and noise levels etc.  I would not trust it.

I treat the the list of identified regions as a first rough guide.  I
prefer to get false positives rather than miss true positive.  The way
we have worked is that we often filter regions out "manually" to get a
smaller list that is later validated by other means.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi David.

You'll have to do the steps separately.

I'm not sure what everyone else in the list does, but I created a
wrapper function (see below 'doEverything') that does the background
adjustment, normalization and plm fitting, all in one go (and I have
options to do exon array analysis).  It might be useful to others.
Basically, you tell it the name of the dataset and the chip type and
that is all it needs to know to trace your directory structure and
find everything it needs.  It returns a list of all the things you
might need (chip effects, quality assessment model, etc.).  For
example, you might do something like to do the quality assessment:

e<-doEverything("my_dataset","HG-U133_Plus_2")
plotNuse(e$qam)

The nice thing about this is that if you've already processed the
data once, it'll whip through all these steps.  However, you can make
it recalculate everything by setting force=T.

As for the actual NUSE calculations, I think you can call it as 'n<-
plotNuse(e$qam)' to get the values (though I've never done this).
Otherwise, you might check the code in
'plotNuse.QualityAssessmentModel'.

Hope that works.
Mark

doEverything<-function
(name,chip,checkChipType=F,doExon=F,doCore=F,force=F,doMerge=F,doResidua
ls=F,doWeights=F,getExpression=F,verbose=Arguments$getVerbose(-8)) {
   cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(name, chipType=chip,
checkChipType=checkChipType)
   if (doCore)
     chip<-paste(chip,",core",sep="")
   cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(chip)
   setCdf(cs, cdf)
   bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs)
   csBC <- process(bc,verbose=verbose,force=force)
   setCdf(csBC, cdf)
   qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
   csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose,force=force) #time required
   setCdf(csN, cdf)
   if (doExon)
     plm <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,mergeGroups=doMerge)
   else
     plm <- RmaPlm(csN)
   fit(plm, verbose=verbose,units=NULL) #time required
   qam <- QualityAssessmentModel(plm)
   chp<-getChipEffectSet(plm)
   d<-NULL; ws<-NULL; rs<-NULL
   if (getExpression) {
     if (!doExon | doMerge)
       d<-getExprs(chp,doExon=F)
     else
       d<-getExprs(chp,doExon=T)
   }
   if (doResiduals)
     rs<-calculateResiduals(plm,verbose=verbose,force=force)
   if (doWeights)
     ws<-calculateWeights(plm,verbose=verbose,force=force)
   list
(name=name,chip=chip,d=d,cs=csN,cdf=cdf,plm=plm,qam=qam,chp=chp,res=rs,w
ts=ws)
}

getExprs <- function(ces,doExon=F, ...) {
   cdf <- getCdf(ces);
   theta <- extractMatrix(ces, ..., returnUgcMap=TRUE);
   ugcMap <- attr(theta, "unitGroupCellMap");
   if (doExon) {
     x<-getFile(ces,1)
     y<-readUnits(x)
     cn<-names(unlist(y,recursive=F))
     rownames(theta) <-cn
   } else {
     un<-getUnitNames(cdf, ugcMap[,"unit"]);
     rownames(theta) <- un
   }
   log2(theta)

}

verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8); timestampOn(verbose)

setCdf(csBC2, cdf)
qn2 <- QuantileNormalization(csBC2, typesToUpdate="pm")
csN2 <- process(qn2, verbose=verbose) #time required
plm2.merge <- ExonRmaPlm(csN2, mergeGroups=TRUE)

Hi,

good that you found out.  It cannot see a straightforward solution to
the issue where multiple unit groups refer to a common set of probes.
This is a problem because it breaks the underlying assumption in the
design that there is a one-to-one map of "input" and "output" cells.
The result is, as you say, that probe affinity estimates, residuals
and weights are overwritten.  In order to deal with this some of the
basic framework needs to be updates and a more generic file structures
is needed.  This is hard.

same cell do:

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("MoEx-1_0-st-v1")

 int [1:5266159] 5994477 2030429 4309592 5663393 340560 115236
967170 2214061 977049 3384045 ...
t <- table(cells)
reps <- t[t > 1]
> reps
   1
1023

So, in this case the cell with index 1 is replicated 1023 times.  With
the CDF that Elizabeth is referring to there will be more replicates.

Hi,
I think for the exon arrays that you don't really want to have a common
set of probes. In what I discovered, this is a mistake (I don't know if
it's from Ken creation of the cdf or Affy's original annotation). For
Mark's situation, it's a bit more questionable since some probes map to
regions of the genome that refseq (or ensemble, etc.) says actually are
parts of multiple genes. But I guess I would argue that you are not
going to be able to easily disintangle this confounding of the two
expression levels (and moving to refseq annotation instead of Affy's is
partly to be able to avoid the problems this creates), so those probes
will mess up your single-gene analysis. So for me (so far) I don't see
any need to actually address this problem other than to perhaps give
warnings/checks of the cdfs to let the user know. Maybe some automatic
way to throw them out of the cdf, but really it's not fair to expect
aroma.affymetrix to deal with the problem. Or perhaps we (Mark and I?)
should develop something specific to exon arrays to ignore replicated
probes, since it seems like it might be rather specific, but perhaps
common, to the exon arrays right now.
Best,
Elizabeth

Hi,
So I have dug a bit and I was just going to characterize the depth of
the multiple probes problem with the core cdf  in case there is anyone
else out there that would like to know. (I haven't looked at the full
set of probesets, though my code would be the same)

There are 522 core probesets (containing 1994 probes) that are assigned
to multiple units. Each of the 522 probesets shows up as an 'singleton'
unit (i.e. a unit with only that probeset as a group) and also in a
longer unit with multiple probesets. There are only 73 units involved,
so some units have a large number of these probesets (as many as 41
probesets in 1 unit with this problem! see table below). If anyone would
like the list of probesets or units that are involved, I can make that
available on the help pages.

As a side note, there was some discussion before about these singleton
units and what should be the group name (whether the group name is just
blank ("") or if the group name is the same as the unit name). In the
core cdf, both seem to occur (not because of my 522 'special' ones above
either); of the 4736 singleton units, 4129 are blank group names and 607
have the group name as the unit name. I don't know if there is a
purposeful distinction here or not.

Best,
Elizabeth

> cdfqc parts be exclusive, or is cdfqc a subset of cdf?
>
> And then what happens to those qc elements? Do they get automatically
> cut out of functions like fitting the genelevel models, etc.?

Hi Elizabeth

Affxparser uses the same terminology as Affy for the probesets. What
we (they) call QC units is _not_ what you are thinking of (I am 100%
sure). QC units in a CDF file is special probesets that
1) do not have a name
2) do not have a block/group structure
The QC units are typically not being read by any software that reads
CDF files (except readCdfQcUnits). They consists of special probes
that are (amongst other stuff) used for gridding of the image: if you
have ever looked at a high-resolution imgae plot you will have noted
that there is a checkerboard pattern along the edge of the chip + also
a chip name embedded in the image. These pixels are coming from QC
probes.

It might be interesting to look at "QC" probes from a statistical QC
perspective, but no-one has done so and their presence is not being
used by any software I know of.

In addition to the QC units Affy also provides (at least on some
chips), units with names such as "AFFX-BioD". These probesets
(depending on the chip and experimental protocol) are more along what
I would think of as quality control probesets: they target special
genes that are added to the hybridization mix and the distribution of
intensities could be considered a proxy for the quality of the chip.
Just the fact that these probesets have names tell us they are not
"QC" units from a tecnhnical Affy CDF file lingo point of view.

So in short , on a normal Affy chip (let us just think gene expression
here) you have qc units (not used by anyone, probably not relevant in
any analysis), special affy probesets with names and "normal"
probesets targeting something.

For Exon arrays I am pretty sure that one of the reasons Ken did not
include QC probesets was the fact that since the chip is so big, some
of the QC probesets were gigantic with 1000's or more probes. These
probesets were problematic due to their size, so I assume Ken just
opted for an exclusion - an easy decision since they are not being
used by anybody.

As stated above, QC units are not being read by almost any software.
Even using affxparser/aroma.affymetrix you need to do special stuff to
access them.

Kasper

[Bcc:ing Benilton; oligo's maintainer]

Hi,

I took out several methods that I haven't been update for a long time
in the last release and one of them was extractSnpFeatureSet().  One
reason for taking such methods out was that they depended on other
packages that has been updated quite a bit and I haven't had a chance
to catch up.  The oligo package is one such package.  [I'll try to
update the group pages soon pointing this out.]

However, the extractSnpFeatureSet() method was simply a wrapper around
oligo's read.celfiles().  All probe-level data in aroma.affymetrix,
including normalized data, are stored in CEL files of the same chip
type as the raw CEL files, i.e. the same CDF is/can be applied.  Note,
if you do not use aroma.affymetrix for preprocessing, there is no
memory advantages or similar of using aroma.affymetrix.

I remember at the time, oligo::read.celfiles() has some problems
reading CEL files from another directory, so one had to set the
working directory to where the CEL files were, and load the data from
there.  If that is still the case, you have/can do like this to load
your data into oligo:

# Assume 'csN' in an AffymetrixCelSet object containing your normalized data.

# Set the working directory to be that of the CEL files
opwd <- setwd(getPath(csN));
# Get the filenames of the CEL files
filenames <- basename(getPathnames(this));
# Load the CEL files into oligo
sfs <- oligo::read.celfiles(filenames);
# Go back to the original working directory
setwd(opwd);

So, 'sfs' now holds you SnpFeatureSet.  Again, as this example,
reveals there is nothing special that aroma.affymetrix would do to
"extract" the data; it simply just loads it using oligo's functions.

BTW, very soon aroma.affymetrix will no longer support R v2.5.1 and
all of Bioconductor already moved to R v2.6.0... so update.

Hope this helps

Henrik

whole data set and then redoing it on a subset.  What is your
statistical model/algorithm you're trying fit?

to specify a subset of arrays.  One reason for this the large risk for
conflicting/overwriting result files, which is what you are
experiencing.  Instead, the idea is to have the result sets being
separated from each others by outputting them in different
directories.  Then, if you later want to merge them together in a
downstream analysis, that can be done using the append() method of
AffymetrixCelSet.

To output your the PLM results for the XX and the XY samples in
different directories, just add a tag to each of them, e.g.

dsNXX <- extract(dsN,xxIdxs);
plm <- RmaCnPlm(dsNXX, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, tags=c("*","XX"))

cesXX <- getChipEffectSet(plm);

fit(plm);
cesXY <- getChipEffectSet(plm);

# Merge the chip-effect sets.
ces <- cesXX;
append(ces, cesXY);
print(ces);

be the one specifying the name and the tags.  To override this, you
can use:

setAlias(ces, 'MyMergedDataset')

setTags() to change the tags.  Default is "*" which expands to
whatever the pathname says it is.

fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
process(fln);

> >
> > > However, the extractSnpFeatureSet() method was simply a wrapper around
> > > oligo's read.celfiles().  All probe-level data in aroma.affymetrix,
> > > including normalized data, are stored in CEL files of the same chip
> > > type as the raw CEL files, i.e. the same CDF is/can be applied.  Note,
> > > if you do not use aroma.affymetrix for preprocessing, there is no
> > > memory advantages or similar of using aroma.affymetrix.
> >
> > > I remember at the time, oligo::read.celfiles() has some problems
> > > reading CEL files from another directory, so one had to set the
> > > working directory to where the CEL files were, and load the data from
> > > there.  If that is still the case, you have/can do like this to load
> > > your data into oligo:
> >
> > > # Assume 'csN' in an AffymetrixCelSet object containing your normalized data.
> >
> > > # Set the working directory to be that of the CEL files
> > > opwd <- setwd(getPath(csN));
> > > # Get the filenames of the CEL files

> >
> >  filenames <- basename(getPathnames(csN));
> >

> > > # Load the CEL files into oligo
> > > sfs <- oligo::read.celfiles(filenames);
> > > # Go back to the original working directory
> > > setwd(opwd);
> >
> > > So, 'sfs' now holds you SnpFeatureSet.  Again, as this example,
